title: Gravitation
tagline: From the equivalence principle to an expanding universe
summary: The equivalence principle, the Schwarzschild geometry, black holes, gravitational waves, the structure of stars, and a first cosmology.
overview: General relativity is the theory of gravitation in which energy and momentum curve spacetime and free fall is motion along a geodesic. This course does not develop the full tensor machinery. It develops the physical content a physics graduate should be able to use: the equivalence principle, the Schwarzschild geometry and its predictions, black holes, gravitational waves at the level of their effect on a detector, and the two great applications, stars and cosmology.

The equivalence principle alone gives the gravitational redshift, the GPS clock correction and half the bending of light, and leads to the idea that gravity is a metric. The Schwarzschild metric is then taken as the spherically symmetric vacuum solution and read for orbits, the innermost stable circular orbit, the precession of Mercury, the deflection of light, the Shapiro delay and, when all the mass is inside $r_s$, the event horizon. Gravitational waves are treated through linearised gravity and the quadrupole formula, tested by the binary pulsar and by GW150914. Stellar structure uses Newtonian hydrostatic equilibrium and the virial theorem, with general relativity entering for neutron stars, and cosmology uses the Friedmann equations with matter, radiation and a cosmological constant.

Several famous formulae in this course, including the Schwarzschild metric, the quadrupole formula and the Hawking temperature, are quoted from the field equations or from quantum field theory rather than derived, and the text says so each time. What is derived is everything that follows from them. The skill to acquire is knowing which predictions are geometry, which are astrophysics, and which numbers come from observation, and being able to compute each to the precision the data deserve.
outcomes: Explain the weak and Einstein equivalence principles and the experimental bounds on the Eötvös parameter.
Derive the gravitational redshift and compute clock-rate corrections such as the 38 μs per day for GPS.
Use the conserved energy and angular momentum of Schwarzschild geodesics to find the effective potential, the ISCO at 6GM/c² and the photon sphere.
Compute the perihelion precession of Mercury, the deflection of starlight by the Sun and the Shapiro delay.
Distinguish coordinate from curvature singularities, describe the event horizon, and compute tidal accelerations, shadow sizes and Hawking temperatures of black holes.
Describe how a gravitational wave moves free test masses, apply the quadrupole formula to a binary, and estimate a chirp mass from the frequency evolution.
Prove the virial theorem for a star and use it with hydrostatic equilibrium to estimate central temperatures and the Kelvin–Helmholtz and nuclear time scales.
Explain degeneracy pressure, the Chandrasekhar limit and the maximum mass of neutron stars.
Derive the Friedmann and fluid equations, and compute redshifts, critical density, cosmological distances and the age of the universe numerically.

history.title: The equivalence principle
history.detail: In a review article of 1907 Einstein argued that a uniform gravitational field is locally indistinguishable from an acceleration, and deduced the gravitational redshift and time dilation from that.

history.title: The field equations
history.detail: Einstein presented the perihelion advance of Mercury to the Prussian Academy on 18 November 1915 and the final field equations on 25 November.

history.title: The Schwarzschild solution
history.detail: Karl Schwarzschild, serving on the Russian front, found the exact spherically symmetric vacuum solution; Einstein presented it to the Academy in January 1916.

history.title: The eclipse
history.detail: Expeditions to Sobral and Príncipe organised by Dyson and Eddington measured the deflection of starlight during the eclipse of 29 May 1919, in agreement with general relativity rather than with the Newtonian half-value.

history.title: The expanding universe
history.detail: Friedmann (1922) and Lemaître (1927) had found expanding solutions of Einstein's equations; Hubble's 1929 paper established that galaxy redshifts grow linearly with distance.

history.title: The Chandrasekhar limit
history.detail: Chandrasekhar showed that relativistic electron degeneracy cannot support a white dwarf above a limiting mass, now put at about 1.4 solar masses. In 1939 Oppenheimer and Volkoff computed the first neutron-star models.

history.title: Redshift in the laboratory
history.detail: Pound and Rebka measured the gravitational redshift of 14.4 keV gamma rays over the 22.5 m height of a Harvard tower using the Mössbauer effect; the result was published in 1960.

history.title: The microwave background
history.detail: Penzias and Wilson found an isotropic microwave background at Bell Laboratories, interpreted by Dicke's group as the relic radiation of a hot early universe.

history.title: The binary pulsar
history.detail: Hulse and Taylor discovered PSR B1913+16, a pulsar orbiting another neutron star; its orbital decay, measured over decades, matches the energy loss to gravitational waves.

history.title: GW150914
history.detail: On 14 September 2015 the two LIGO detectors recorded the merger of black holes of about 36 and 29 solar masses; the announcement came on 11 February 2016. In 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope published the first image of a black hole's shadow, in M87.

references.title: Gravity: An Introduction to Einstein’s General Relativity
references.note: The book this course follows: physics first, with the Schwarzschild geometry used before the field equations are derived.

references.title: A First Course in General Relativity
references.note: Third edition. More tensor machinery than Hartle, and the natural next step.

references.title: Spacetime and Geometry
references.note: A graduate text (reissued by Cambridge University Press in 2019). The early chapters are a clear account of the geometry used here; chapters 5, 6 and 8 treat the Schwarzschild solution, black holes and cosmology.

references.title: Gravitation
references.authors: Charles W. Misner, Kip S. Thorne and John Archibald Wheeler
references.note: The encyclopaedic classic. Its boxed physical discussions of the classical tests, stellar structure and gravitational waves reward browsing long after the course.

references.title: An Introduction to Modern Astrophysics
references.authors: Bradley W. Carroll and Dale A. Ostlie
references.note: Second edition (Pearson, 2007; reissued by Cambridge University Press in 2017). The chapters on stellar interiors, degenerate stars and cosmology, for the astrophysical half.

references.title: Introduction to Cosmology
references.note: Second edition. A short, careful cosmology at the level of the last chapter.
